1.pericope_label: Bow down thine ear, O Lord, hear me: for I am poor and needy

schools.summary: Augustine makes the psalm the prayer of the whole Christ, since God gave no greater gift than to make his Word the head of men and join them to him as members, so that Christ prays for us as priest, prays in us as head, and is prayed to by us as God.

Calvin refers the psalm to the persecution by Saul while allowing it may have been written afterwards in leisure, and holds that nothing is more suitable to the nature of God than to succour the afflicted, the most destitute being the most surely helped; Gill applies the petition for preservation to Christ, whose life was kept in infancy and in the wilderness and from those who sought it before his time.

Spurgeon finds the plea in the weakness itself, misery being the master argument with mercy, and rebukes those who repeat such words in public worship while despising the poor; Henry counts the plainness of the language a merit, since the flourishes of wit are not the proper ornaments of prayer, and notes that every passage here is addressed to God rather than to hearers.

Clarke accepts the title only so far, holding the structure like that of the Korahite psalms and the date probably the captivity, reads the disputed word actively as merciful and sums the prayer in a couplet asking that the mercy shown to others be shown to him; Wesley narrows the same word to sincere devotion to God’s service.

Ellicott renders the disputed word as one of the chosen ones, making the plea rest on the covenant relation rather than on character; Keil and Delitzsch deny the psalm to David on grounds of poetical capability, call it more liturgic than poetic, catalogue its borrowings from earlier psalms and the Law, and note that one divine name occurs in it seven times.

debates: Who wrote this psalm? Clarke accepts that the title and all the versions give it to David but finds its structure the same as the Korahite psalms and its date probably the captivity; Keil and Delitzsch deny it to David on the ground that the writer cannot be compared with him for poetical capability, and support the denial with a catalogue of borrowings from earlier psalms and the Law; Calvin keeps David and refers it to the persecution by Saul, though possibly written later in peace.

What is claimed by the words for I am holy? Clarke translates the word actively as merciful, so that the psalmist asks only for the mercy he himself shows; Ellicott keeps the passive sense but grounds it in election, one of the chosen ones, so that the covenant and not the character is pleaded; Wesley reduces it to sincere devotion to God’s service.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch judge the poem inferior for the very plainness that Henry praises, the one calling it more liturgic than purely poetic and the other observing that the flourishes of wit are not the proper ornaments of prayer.

Spurgeon says that the language of spiritual poverty sounds like a mockery of the Most High when repeated in the public congregation by great ones of the earth who count the peasantry little better than the earth they tread upon.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the divine name used here occurs seven times in the psalm, and record the disagreement of editors over two places where a different name has been printed.
themes: a title accepted, doubted and dated three ways
plainness read as poetic weakness and as fitness for prayer
a claim to holiness softened into a claim to mercy
weakness urged as the argument that moves mercy
the psalm heard as the prayer of the whole Christ

5.pericope_label: For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive: in the day of my trouble I will call upon thee

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes essential, providential and gracious goodness in the fifth verse, notes that the psalmist calls the prayer his own composition and repeats it out of importunity, and gives an anatomy of the sources of trouble, from a man’s own corruptions, from persecutors and false teachers, from Satan, and from the hand of God itself, adding that such troubles are for a day only.

Clarke rests the plea on God’s goodness and on the character all his followers attest, counts three marks of the psalmist’s earnestness in that he prayed, prayed vehemently and continued in prayer, and puts the request at its bluntest, that millions call for mercy but none has more need than himself.

Ellicott marks the turn from pleading need to appealing to the nature of God, traces the language of the fifth verse to the older revelations of that nature, and dwells on a word for forgiveness found nowhere else in this form, which the Greek version renders by a term implying that legal right is suspended in consideration of human weakness; Keil and Delitzsch place the speaker among the persecuted of the time of Saul.

outliers: Ellicott finds the nearest English equivalent for the Greek rendering of ready to forgive in the word considerate, taken as meaning that legal right is overlooked and suspended out of regard for human weakness.
Clarke reduces the plea to a single blunt comparison, that millions call upon God for help and mercy but that none has more need than the man praying.
Gill lists the professors of religion alongside profane sinners among the causes of a good man’s trouble.
themes: the plea shifting from the suppliant to the nature of God
forgiveness described as right suspended for weakness
importunity counted a mark of earnestness
trouble traced to four separate sources
trouble bounded by a day

8.pericope_label: Among the gods there is none like unto thee: unite my heart to fear thy name

schools.summary: Spurgeon divides the gods into those holding delegated office and those nominated by superstition, and supposes that even if every imaginary deity became really divine he would still choose this God and reject the rest; Henry allows the nations a partial fulfilment in the proselytes of the days of David and Solomon and reserves the full accomplishment for the days of the Messiah.

Gill identifies the gods as angels, as magistrates, or as the fictitious deities of the nations, argues that he who made the nations is able to make them do homage, reads the petition for teaching as a request for further instruction in a way already known, and takes praise with the whole heart to express sincerity rather than perfection.

Clarke tests the gods by their record, that none who trusted an idol was ever helped or answered, makes the coming of the nations a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles attested by miracles, expounds the prayer for a united heart at length as the cure for scattered affections, and insists the last verse means more than the grave, a hell below hell; Wesley compresses the same prayer to knitting the whole heart to God and glosses the last phrase as extreme dangers.

Ellicott marks the move from confidence that God will hear to confidence that he can save, traces the language to older psalms, reads the united heart as the concentration of all the powers on one service, and denies that the last verse implies any comparison, taking it of the underworld beneath and, from the following verse, of danger of death by violence.

debates: What does it mean to be delivered from the lowest hell? Clarke holds the phrase must mean more than the grave and names a place of perdition for the soul as the grave is a place of corruption for the body, calling it a hell below hell; Ellicott denies that any comparison is implied, renders the words as the underworld beneath, and argues from the next verse that the danger meant is simply death by violence; Wesley glosses it as extreme dangers and miseries.

When will all nations come and worship? Henry finds a partial fulfilment in the proselytes of the days of David and Solomon and reserves the rest for the days of the Messiah; Clarke makes the verse a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, attested by the miracles of Christ; Spurgeon grounds it in creation, since all mankind descend from the first man and every life is a distinct creation.
outliers: Spurgeon supposes that if every imaginary deity could start into actual existence and become really divine, he would still choose the God of this psalm and reject all the others.

Clarke calls the prayer for a united heart a most important one, holding that a divided heart is a great curse, that scattered affections are a miserable plague, and that the heart must be one in order that the work may be one.
Clarke tests the gods by their record rather than their nature, since none who trusted in an idol ever had help in time of need and none who prayed to one ever had an answer.
themes: incomparability argued from works rather than from rank
the nations owed to God as their maker
a divided will named as the obstacle to religion
deliverance from a depth variously located
praise offered with the whole heart as sincerity

14.pericope_label: O God, the proud are risen against me: but thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion

schools.summary: Spurgeon holds that none hate good men so fiercely as the high-minded, that persecutors hunt in packs, and that those who do not fear God are not afraid to be cruel, an atheist being a misanthrope; he calls the description of God a doxology without one redundant word and distributes its terms among the weak, the undeserving, the provoking, the guilty and the tried.

Gill reports a Jewish commentator applying the proud to two named persecutors of David, takes the compassion of the fifteenth verse as that of a mother to the son of her womb, reads the hiding of God’s face behind the plea to turn, and notes a reading that referred the token asked for to the kingdom itself.

Clarke turns the last clause of the fourteenth verse into two questions about the consciousness of the divine presence, glosses each word of the doxology in the original and finds the older English tongue too scanty to render them, traces the word knave from a neutral term for a serving man through the dishonesty of servants, and reads the token asked for as the marking of a slave to establish whose property he was.

Ellicott notes that the fourteenth verse is taken bodily from an earlier psalm, holds that the combined expressions servant and son of thine handmaid imply a homeborn slave, and describes the token asked for as a sign of providential care such as the devout still see in what to others is an every-day occurrence.

outliers: Clarke traces the descent of the word knave from a neutral term for a serving man or a male child, holding that it sank because so many servants were found to be purloiners of their masters’ property, exactly as the Latin word for thief became the ordinary name for a dishonest servant; he supports this from an eclogue asking what masters will do when servants dare such things, and from a comic dramatist’s joke calling a man a fellow of three letters.

Clarke says the scanty language of our ancestors was not adequate to render the divine attributes of the fifteenth verse, and quotes two old English versions in evidence, one calling God mild and mildhearted and of much mildheartedness, the other mercier and sufferand and of mykel mercy.
Spurgeon calls the description of God a doxology with no redundant word and says that love is one and yet sevenfold, its white ray containing the whole scale of colours.
Clarke reports that the old paraphrase read the handmaid of the sixteenth verse as the church and her son as the true believer.
themes: persecution treated as evidence of irreligion
a doxology parcelled out among kinds of need
the poverty of an older tongue for the divine attributes
a word for servant degraded into a word for rogue
a sign asked for that enemies could also read
